h: From Buckingham House to royal HQ
p: The palace didn't start out royal at all. It began life as Buckingham House, built in 1703 for the Duke of Buckingham. George III bought it in 1761 as a family home for Queen Charlotte, and it was later massively extended. Queen Victoria was the first monarch to make it her official London home, moving in soon after she came to the throne in 1837, and it has been the centre of royal life ever since.

If you do get inside during the summer opening, allow a couple of hours. The visit takes you through the State Rooms and usually finishes with a walk in part of the palace garden, which is a real treat right in the middle of London.

Even when the doors are shut, there's plenty to see. The Changing the Guard ceremony takes place on the palace forecourt on set days, drawing big crowds, so arrive early if you want a decent spot at the railings and check the schedule before you go. The Victoria Memorial in front of the palace gives a good vantage point too.

The Royal Mews, the working stables and carriage house round the side of the palace, is a separate attraction where you can see the state coaches, including the dazzling Gold State Coach. It's often a hit with kids.

Then make a walk of it. Stroll up The Mall towards Trafalgar Square, or wander through St James's Park, with its lake, wildfowl and famous pelicans. Green Park sits on the other side of the palace, and Westminster Abbey and the Houses of Parliament are within easy walking distance.
